title: Measuring risk and risk-adjusted return
objectives: Define standard deviation, beta, Sharpe, Treynor and alpha.
Choose a measure for a comparison.
body_md:
Return alone hides risk. Use these measures.

| Measure | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Standard deviation** | Volatility of returns; higher means more risk |
| **Beta** | Sensitivity to the market; 1 = moves with the market, above 1 = more volatile |
| **R-squared** | How closely the fund tracks its benchmark |
| **Sharpe ratio** | (Fund return − risk-free rate) ÷ standard deviation; return per unit of total risk |
| **Treynor ratio** | (Fund return − risk-free rate) ÷ beta; return per unit of market risk |
| **Alpha** | Excess return over what the beta predicted; positive means the manager added value |
| **Tracking error** | Standard deviation of the gap between fund and benchmark; low for index funds |

## Use

- Higher Sharpe is better; compare funds in the same category.
- An index fund should have **low tracking error**.
- A **Riskometer** summarises risk in six levels from Low to Very High.

## Example

Fund A: return 14%, risk-free 6%, standard deviation 16%: Sharpe = (14 − 6) ÷ 16 = **0.5**.

> **Exam tip:** Sharpe uses standard deviation; Treynor uses beta.
